result:
A connection pool keeps a set of already-open database connections alive and lends them out to requests, instead of opening a new connection each time. When your code needs the database it borrows a connection from the pool, runs its queries, and returns it; the connection stays open for the next borrower. If all connections are in use, the caller waits until one is returned or a timeout fires.

It helps because opening a connection is expensive: a TCP handshake, usually TLS, authentication, and on the server side allocating a session (in Postgres, a whole process). That can cost several milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, often more than the query itself, so reusing connections removes that cost from every request.

It also caps the number of connections the database sees. Databases degrade badly when thousands of clients connect at once, since each connection consumes memory and contends for CPU and locks, so a fixed pool size turns a traffic spike into a short queue in your application rather than an overloaded database.

The main thing to get right is pool size: too small and requests queue for a connection, too large and you lose the protection. A small number (roughly a few times the database's core count, summed across all your application instances) usually beats a large one. Also make sure connections are always returned, because a leaked connection is permanently lost capacity and eventually the pool is exhausted.
